Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of $\mathcal A$-measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. For a fixed sample $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathcal Z^m$, where $m\ge1$, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Define

$$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U$ be a nonempty subset of the real matrix space $\mathbb R^{n\times m}$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A **proper $\epsilon$-cover** of $U$ in Frobenius norm is a finite subset $V\subseteq U$ such that every $X\in U$ has some $Y\in V$ with $\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\le\epsilon$. The **proper Frobenius covering number** $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least cardinality of such a cover when one exists, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The cover is proper because its centers belong to $U$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: For $x>0$, put $r(x)=x-\tanh x$. By [F3], $r(0)=0$ and $r'(x)=1-\operatorname{sech}^2x=\tanh^2x\ge0$. The mean value theorem [F6] therefore gives $r(x)\ge0$; at $x=0$ this is equality. Put $q(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\cosh x$. The derivative rules in [F3] and [F7] give $q'(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\cosh x\,(\tanh x-x)\le0$. Applying [F6] on $[0,x]$ for $x>0$ yields $q(x)\le q(0)=1$, and equality holds at $x=0$. Since $q$ is even, $\cosh x\le e^{x^2/2}$ for every real $x$.

Choose $g_0\in\mathcal G$ and subtract its sample vector $v_0$ from every vector in $\mathcal G|S$. The empirical Rademacher average is unchanged because $\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sum_i\varepsilon_i g_0(z_i)=0$, and translation preserves all Frobenius covering numbers. Write $U:=(\mathcal G|S)-v_0$; it contains $0$, and each vector has norm at most $\sqrt n$. For any $\epsilon>0$, partition $[-1,1]^n$ into finitely many boxes of side at most $\epsilon/\sqrt n$; from each box meeting $U$ take one member of that intersection. The resulting finite set is a proper $\epsilon$-cover, since two points in one box differ in Euclidean norm by at most $\epsilon$. Set $\epsilon_j=\sqrt n\,2^{-(j-1)}$. The singleton $V_1=\{0\}$ is a proper $\epsilon_1$-cover of $U$, so $|V_1|=N_F(U,\epsilon_1)=1$. For each finite truncation $N\ge2$ and each $2\le j\le N$, choose a proper $\epsilon_j$-cover $V_j$ of $U$ with the least possible cardinality, so $|V_j|=N_F(U,\epsilon_j)$; such a least cardinality exists because a finite cover exists and cover cardinalities are positive integers. Enumerate each finite cover and map every sample vector to the first center within $\epsilon_j$.

Let $V$ be a nonempty finite set of vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ and let $R=\max_{v\in V}\lVert v\rVert_2$. For $T_v=\sum_i\varepsilon_i v_i$, independence of the signs and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda T_v}=\prod_i\cosh(\lambda v_i)\le e^{\lambda^2R^2/2}$. If $R=0$ or $|V|=1$, $\mathbb E\max_{v\in V}T_v=0$. Otherwise, for $\lambda>0$, [F4] and $e^{\lambda\max_v T_v}\le\sum_{v\in V}e^{\lambda T_v}$ imply $\mathbb E\max_vT_v\le\log|V|/\lambda+\lambda R^2/2$. Choosing $\lambda=\sqrt{2\log|V|}/R$ gives $\mathbb E\max_vT_v\le R\sqrt{2\log|V|}$.

For any translated sample vector $v\in U$, telescope $v=(v-v_N[v])+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}(v_{j+1}[v]-v_j[v])$, since $v_1[v]=0$. The absolute residual sign sum is at most $\lVert(\varepsilon_i)_i\rVert_2\lVert v-v_N[v]\rVert_2\le\sqrt n\epsilon_N$ by [F8]. For each $j<N$, use only the paired-center difference set $D_j:=\{v_{j+1}[v]-v_j[v]:v\in U\}$. It is a nonempty subset of $V_{j+1}-V_j$, so its cardinality is at most $|V_{j+1}||V_j|\le N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon_{j+1})^2$, because covering numbers are nonincreasing with radius. Each paired difference has norm at most $\lVert v_{j+1}[v]-v\rVert_2+\lVert v-v_j[v]\rVert_2\le\epsilon_{j+1}+\epsilon_j=3\epsilon_{j+1}$. Step 2.1 applied to $D_j$ therefore bounds its expected maximum sign sum by $6\epsilon_{j+1}\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon_{j+1})}$. Taking the supremum in the telescoping identity, summing these bounds, and dividing by $n$ gives $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le\epsilon_N/\sqrt n+(6/n)\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\epsilon_{j+1}\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon_{j+1})}$.

The function $f(\epsilon)=\sqrt{\log N_F(\mathcal G|S,\epsilon)}$ is nonincreasing in $\epsilon$. Since $\epsilon_{j+2}=\epsilon_{j+1}/2$, each summand obeys $\epsilon_{j+1}f(\epsilon_{j+1})\le2\int_{\epsilon_{j+2}}^{\epsilon_{j+1}}f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon$. Therefore step 3.1 gives $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le\epsilon_N/\sqrt n+(12/n)\int_{\epsilon_{N+1}}^{\sqrt n}f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon$.

If $\sqrt n/4\le\alpha\le\sqrt n$, each signed average is at most $1$, so $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le1\le4\alpha/\sqrt n$. If $0<\alpha<\sqrt n/4$, choose the largest $N\ge1$ with $\epsilon_{N+1}>\alpha$; such an $N$ exists because $\epsilon_2=\sqrt n/2>\alpha$ and $\epsilon_j\to0$. Maximality gives $\epsilon_{N+2}\le\alpha$, hence $\epsilon_N=4\epsilon_{N+2}\le4\alpha$, and $\int_{\epsilon_{N+1}}^{\sqrt n}f\le\int_\alpha^{\sqrt n}f$. Substitution into step 4.1 proves the stated inequality for every $0<\alpha<\sqrt n/4$. Together, the two cases prove it for every $0<\alpha\le\sqrt n$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U$ be a nonempty subset of the real matrix space $\mathbb R^{n\times m}$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A **proper $\epsilon$-cover** of $U$ in Frobenius norm is a finite subset $V\subseteq U$ such that every $X\in U$ has some $Y\in V$ with $\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\le\epsilon$. The **proper Frobenius covering number** $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least cardinality of such a cover when one exists, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The cover is proper because its centers belong to $U$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: For any $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, write its columns as $b_j$ and the columns of $X$ as $x_r$. By [F2], $\lVert Xb_j\rVert_2^2=\sum_i|\sum_rX_{ir}(b_j)_r|^2\le\lVert X\rVert_F^2\lVert b_j\rVert_2^2$. Summing over $j$ gives $\lVert XB\rVert_F\le\lVert X\rVert_F(\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert_2^2)^{1/2}\le\lVert X\rVert_F\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert_2=\lVert X\rVert_F\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}$; the middle inequality follows by squaring, since all column norms are nonnegative. Thus $\lVert A-A'\rVert_{2,1}\le2a$ for $A,A'\in C$, and the diameter of $U$ is at most $2a\lVert X\rVert_F$. If $a\lVert X\rVert_F=0$, $U$ is a singleton; if $\epsilon\ge2a\lVert X\rVert_F$, any one point of nonempty $U$ covers it.

Assume $a\lVert X\rVert_F>0$ and $0<\epsilon<2a\lVert X\rVert_F$. For each nonzero column $x_r$, each output coordinate $j$, and each sign $\eta\in\{-1,+1\}$, form the rank-one atom $V_{rj\eta}=\eta(x_r/\lVert x_r\rVert_2)e_j^\top$, where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector in $\mathbb R^m$. There are at most $2dm$ atoms and each has Frobenius norm $1$. For $B=A-M$, the expansion $XB=\sum_{r,j}(B)_{rj}x_re_j^\top$ has coefficient mass $\beta:=\sum_{r,j}|B_{rj}|\lVert x_r\rVert_2\le\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}\lVert X\rVert_F\le a\lVert X\rVert_F=:c$, by [F2] column by column. Hence $XB/c$ lies in the convex hull of these signed atoms: if $\beta<c$, fill the remaining weight with $0$, which is the midpoint of an atom and its negative. If $\beta=0$, the product is $0$.

For an integer $k\ge1$, sample $k$ atoms independently from the finite convex representation of $XB/c$ constructed in step 1.2. If $V_1,\ldots,V_k$ are these atoms and $\mathbb E V_1=XB/c$, expansion of the squared Frobenius norm and independence give $\mathbb E\lVert c k^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^kV_t-XB\rVert_F^2=(c^2/k)(\mathbb E\lVert V_1\rVert_F^2-\lVert\mathbb EV_1\rVert_F^2)\le c^2/k$. Therefore some ordered $k$-tuple gives a center within $c/\sqrt k$, and all such centers number at most $(2dm)^k$. Taking $k=\lceil c^2/\epsilon^2\rceil$ yields an external $\epsilon$-cover of the translated relaxed product set $XM+\{XB:\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}\le a\}$.

The mixed-norm constraint set is convex: for $A,A'\in C$ and $0\le t\le1$, the column triangle inequality [F3] gives $\lVert t(A-M)+(1-t)(A'-M)\rVert_{2,1}\le ta+(1-t)a=a$. The operator-norm constraint is convex because for each unit vector $v$, $\lVert(tA+(1-t)A')v\rVert_2\le t\lVert Av\rVert_2+(1-t)\lVert A'v\rVert_2\le s$, and taking the supremum over $v$ preserves the bound. The mixed norm is continuous as a finite sum of continuous column norms. From [F7] and the Euclidean triangle inequality, $|\lVert A\rVert_\sigma-\lVert A'\rVert_\sigma|\le\lVert A-A'\rVert_\sigma\le\lVert A-A'\rVert_F$, where the last inequality follows from the rowwise Cauchy estimate in step 1.1; hence the operator norm is continuous and $C$ is closed. Also $\lVert A-M\rVert_F\le\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}\le a$, so $C$ is bounded. By [F5], $C$ is compact; its linear image $U$ is compact and convex. Project each external center $z$ from step 2.1 to a nearest point $p$ of $U$, which exists by compactness. For any $u\in U$, convexity gives $p+t(u-p)\in U$ for $0\le t\le1$. Put $\langle P,Q\rangle_F:=\sum_{i,j}P_{ij}Q_{ij}$. Minimality implies $0\le\lVert z-p-t(u-p)\rVert_F^2-\lVert z-p\rVert_F^2=-2t\langle z-p,u-p\rangle_F+t^2\lVert u-p\rVert_F^2$ for $t>0$; division by $t$ and passage to $t\downarrow0$ give $\langle z-p,u-p\rangle_F\le0$. Expanding $\lVert z-u\rVert_F^2$ then gives $\lVert p-u\rVert_F^2\le\lVert z-u\rVert_F^2$. Thus projection does not increase distance to any point of $U$, and the cover becomes proper without increasing its size.

Put $q=a^2\lVert X\rVert_F^2/\epsilon^2>1/4$. Then $k=\lceil q\rceil\le q+1\le5q$, so step 2.1 and [F6] imply $\log N_F(U,\epsilon)\le k\log(2dm)\le5q\log(2dm)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves both cases of the Statement.

Let $K\ge2$, let $D$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and let $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^K$ be a continuous score map. At $(x,y)$ its **multiclass margin** is
$$m_F(x,y):=F(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}F(x)_j.$$
The predicted label is the smallest index maximizing $F(x)_j$. Its population zero-one error is
$$L_0(F):=D\bigl(\{(x,y):\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le j\le K}F(x)_j\ne y\}\bigr).$$
For $\gamma>0$, the **ramp loss** is
$$\ell_\gamma(r):=\begin{cases}0,&r< -\gamma,\\1+r/\gamma,&-\gamma\le r\le0,\\1,&r>0.\end{cases}$$
The population ramp risk is $R_\gamma(F):=\int\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))\,D(d(x,y))$. For a sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ of length $n\ge1$, the empirical ramp risk and empirical margin loss are
$$\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x_i,y_i)),\qquad\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{m_F(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The score coordinates are continuous, and finite maxima, comparisons, and the piecewise-linear ramp preserve Borel measurability. Thus the classification event and ramp loss in the displayed integrals are Borel sets or functions, so the risks are well-defined for $D$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward ([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of $\mathcal A$-measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. For a fixed sample $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathcal Z^m$, where $m\ge1$, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Define

$$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

derivations.claim: Let $\Theta$ be the set of all feasible tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_L)$. The mixed-norm constraints are closed because each is a finite sum of continuous Euclidean column norms. For each layer, $\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$ is the intersection, over all unit vectors $v$, of the closed conditions $\lVert A_iv\rVert_2\le s_i$, by the induced-operator-norm definition. Each column $A_ie_j$ then has norm at most $s_i$, so all matrix entries are bounded. Hence $\Theta$ is closed and bounded in finite-dimensional Euclidean space and is compact by [F2].

For fixed $x$, induction over the layers shows that the score vector depends continuously on the matrix tuple: matrix multiplication is jointly continuous and each Lipschitz activation is continuous. Finite maxima, coordinate differences, and the ramp preserve continuity, so for fixed $(x,y)$ the loss $A\mapsto\ell_\gamma(-m_{F_A}(x,y))$ is continuous. If $A^{(r)}\to A$, these losses converge pointwise in $(x,y)$ and are bounded by one, so [F3] shows that $A\mapsto R_\gamma(F_A)$ is continuous. Each empirical loss and each finite signed sum of losses is also continuous in $A$.

Identify the parameter tuples with $\mathbb R^p$, where $p:=\sum_{i=1}^L d_i d_{i-1}$. The balls $B(q,r)$ with $q\in\mathbb Q^p$ and $r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$ form a countable family: each rational is a quotient of an integer by a positive integer, the integers have the enumeration $0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots$, and finite tuples of natural numbers are enumerated by iterating the diagonal pairing $\pi(a,b):=(a+b)(a+b+1)/2+b$. They form a base because for any open $O\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $x\in O$, choose $\eta>0$ with $B(x,\eta)\subseteq O$, then use [F9] in each coordinate interval $(x_j-\eta/(4\sqrt p),x_j+\eta/(4\sqrt p))$ to choose $q\in\mathbb Q^p$ with $\lVert q-x\rVert_2<\eta/4$. Use [F9] again to choose a rational $r$ with $\lVert q-x\rVert_2<r<\eta-\lVert q-x\rVert_2$ (a nonempty interval with positive upper endpoint); then $x\in B(q,r)\subseteq B(x,\eta)\subseteq O$. Intersecting these balls with $\Theta$ gives a countable base for its subspace topology. Using [F5], choose one point of $\Theta$ from each nonempty basic intersection; the selected countable subset is dense in $\Theta$. By step 2.1, each supremum over $\Theta$ defining the uniform deviation or a signed empirical supremum equals the supremum over this countable dense subset. The losses are Borel in $(x,y)$ because the scores are continuous in $x$, the margin is a finite maximum of continuous coordinates, and the label set is finite. These countable suprema are therefore measurable.

Write $Z(S):=\sup_{F\in\mathcal F}(R_\gamma(F)-\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F))$. Let $S'$ be an independent ghost sample from $D$. By the integral identities in [F4] and the inequality $\sup_F\mathbb E_{S'}U_F\le\mathbb E_{S'}\sup_F U_F$, $\mathbb E Z(S)\le\mathbb E_{S,S'}\sup_{F\in\mathcal F}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(\ell_F(x_i',y_i')-\ell_F(x_i,y_i)\bigr),$ where $\ell_F(x,y)=\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))$. Swapping each iid pair $(z_i,z_i')$ leaves its law unchanged; introducing independent uniform signs $\varepsilon_i$ therefore leaves this expectation unchanged when each difference is multiplied by $\varepsilon_i$. The supremum of a sum is at most the sum of the suprema, and symmetry of the signs gives $\mathbb E Z(S)\le2\mathbb E_S\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)$.

Replacing one sample coordinate changes $Z(S)$ by at most $1/n$, since every loss lies in $[0,1]$; it also changes $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)$ by at most $1/n$, by [F7] and the same range bound. Apply the upper-tail bound [F6] to $Z$ and to $-\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)$, each with failure probability $\delta/2$ and $t=\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}$. Outside a set of probability at most $\delta$, both $Z(S)\le\mathbb EZ(S)+t$ and $\mathbb E\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)\le\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+t$. Combining with step 4.1 gives $Z(S)\le\mathbb EZ(S)+t\le2\mathbb E\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+t\le2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal L_\gamma)+3t$.

If the predicted label differs from $y$, some competing score is at least the true-label score, so $m_F(x,y)\le0$ and $\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))=1$. Hence the zero-one loss is pointwise at most the ramp loss. Also $\ell_\gamma(-m)\le\mathbf1\{m\le\gamma\}$ for every real $m$, so empirical ramp risk is at most empirical margin loss. Apply the definition of $Z(S)$ and step 5.1 to conclude the stated bound for every $F\in\mathcal F$ simultaneously.

Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ with $n,d,m\ge1$, and let $a,s\ge0$. Suppose
$$C:=\{A\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}:\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}\le a,\ \lVert A\rVert_\sigma\le s\}$$
is nonempty. Put $U:=\{XA:A\in C\}$. For every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\log N_F(U,\epsilon)\le5\,\frac{a^2\lVert X\rVert_F^2}{\epsilon^2}\log(2dm).$$
If $a\lVert X\rVert_F=0$ or $\epsilon\ge2a\lVert X\rVert_F$, then $N_F(U,\epsilon)=1$. Here $\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}$ is the column-sum norm of the transpose-difference, as fixed in the spectral-network-complexity definition, and $N_F$ is the proper Frobenius covering number.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U$ be a nonempty subset of the real matrix space $\mathbb R^{n\times m}$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A **proper $\epsilon$-cover** of $U$ in Frobenius norm is a finite subset $V\subseteq U$ such that every $X\in U$ has some $Y\in V$ with $\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\le\epsilon$. The **proper Frobenius covering number** $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least cardinality of such a cover when one exists, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The cover is proper because its centers belong to $U$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

derivations.claim: Write $Z_i(A)$ for the matrix of rowwise layer-$i$ activations, with $Z_0(A)=X$. Induction gives $\lVert Z_{i-1}(A)\rVert_F\le\lVert X\rVert_F\prod_{j<i}\rho_js_j$: rowwise zero-origin Lipschitzness gives $\lVert Z_i\rVert_F\le\rho_i\lVert Z_{i-1}A_i^\top\rVert_F$, and [F6] identifies $\lVert A_i^\top\rVert_\sigma=\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$, so the induced norm gives $\lVert Z_{i-1}A_i^\top\rVert_F\le s_i\lVert Z_{i-1}\rVert_F$, row by row.

If every $b_i=0$, each feasible layer set is the singleton $\{M_i\}$, so $\mathcal H_X$ is a singleton and the right side is zero. Otherwise set $r_i=b_i/s_i$, $T:=\sum_{i:r_i>0}r_i^{2/3}$, and $\alpha_i:=r_i^{2/3}/T$ for positive $r_i$, with $\alpha_i=0$ when $r_i=0$. These weights are nonnegative and sum to one over the varying layers.

Build finite proper covers of the attainable layer outputs successively. At layer $i$, suppose the previous attainable activation matrices have a proper $\eta$-cover with centers $V$ that are themselves attainable prefix outputs. For each such $V$, [F6] gives $\lVert A_i^\top\rVert_\sigma=\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma$, so apply [F2] to $\{VA_i^\top:A_i\in C_i\}$ with input $V$, reference $M_i^\top$, radius $e_i/\rho_i$, and $e_i:=\alpha_i\epsilon/\prod_{j>i}\rho_js_j$ when $b_i>0$. Map each product-cover center through the rowwise activation $\sigma_i$. Every resulting center is attainable by joining the prefix that realizes $V$ to its feasible layer matrix. For any actual prefix $Z$ within $\eta$ of $V$ and any $A_i\in C_i$, the activation output differs from $\sigma_i(VA_i^\top)$ by at most $\rho_i s_i\eta$; the layer cover adds at most $e_i$. Thus the next-stage cover radius is at most $\rho_i s_i\eta+e_i$. When $b_i=0$, use the single matrix $M_i$ and set $e_i=0$.

is nonempty. Let $\mathcal H_X$ be the set of $n\times d_L$ score matrices whose $r$th row is $F_A(x_r)^\top$, for $A_i\in C_i$ and the $r$th row $x_r^\top$ of $X$. Then for every $\epsilon>0$,
$$\log N_F(\mathcal H_X,\epsilon)\le5\,\frac{\lVert X\rVert_F^2}{\epsilon^2}\log(2W^2)\left(\prod_{i=1}^L(\rho_i s_i)^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^3.$$
The logarithm is natural, an empty product equals $1$, and $N_F$ uses proper centers in the covered score-matrix set.

$$m_F(x,y):=F(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}F(x)_j.$$
The predicted label is the smallest index maximizing $F(x)_j$. Its population zero-one error is
$$L_0(F):=D\bigl(\{(x,y):\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le j\le K}F(x)_j\ne y\}\bigr).$$
For $\gamma>0$, the **ramp loss** is
$$\ell_\gamma(r):=\begin{cases}0,&r< -\gamma,\\1+r/\gamma,&-\gamma\le r\le0,\\1,&r>0.\end{cases}$$
The population ramp risk is $R_\gamma(F):=\int\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))\,D(d(x,y))$. For a sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ of length $n\ge1$, the empirical ramp risk and empirical margin loss are
$$\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x_i,y_i)),\qquad\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{m_F(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.
